text: 20 under the name F-pen-hing. The first, which we have already alludea to, the original of which was lost so early as the beginning of the Tang dynasty, was in five chaptersy(ciouen). There is allusion to another translation (Kat-yuen-shi-kiau-mu-lu, vol. i. chap. 1, ful. 38), bearing the same name but in one chapter, now lost. Again, it is stated (vol. ii, chap. xiii, fol. ॐ , and vol. iii, chap. xx, fol. 3? op. cit.) that a work called ' का sho-hing-tsan-king-fu,' in five chapters, composed originally by Asvagosha, and translated into Chinese by Dharmalatsin, an Indian priest of the Northern Liang dynasty (502-555 a. v.), is also called by many writers Fo-pen-hing. Again (vol. ii, chap. xiii, fol. 2,1, op. ect), it is said that a work called Fv-pen-hiny-king, in seven chapters, was translated by a Shaman of Liang-Chau (called Latnumegha, chap. xx, fol. 42, op. cit.), of the Sung dynasty (420-477.a. p.). The writerthen adds that this last-named translation is sometimes called Lopen-hing-tsan-king."* According to the classification of the Kéhgyur the Lalita Vistara comes under the fifth head of dldo-sde, or aphorisms (Sanskrit, Sutrdnta) of which it forms the second-volume. The Nepalese likewise call it a Satranta, but by the rules of their arrangement it falls under the head of Vyakarana of the class called Gdthé. What this Gatha is, I shall notice in the sequel. Like the rest of the Satra works of the Buddhists, the Lalita Vistara does not record the name of its author.
